mainTopic: Judging others favorably (דן לכף זכות) through three stories, then the משנה's list of foods that may be moved on שבת
overview: This amud opens by finishing an earlier question. A ברייתא listed more rewarding good deeds than the משנה did, and the גמרא explains that the extra items already fit inside the משנה's shorter list. Next, a ברייתא teaches that one who judges others favorably (לכף זכות) is judged favorably by Heaven. Three stories show this in action: a worker who trusts his employer even though he is refused his wages, students who trust a חסיד who kept a ransomed girl near him, and students who trust רבי יהושע after his private meeting with a Roman matron. Each story ends with the same oath and the blessing 'just as you judged me favorably, may ה׳ judge you favorably.' The גמרא then returns to the משנה's list of foods that may be moved on שבת. It explains why each item had to be mentioned: תרומה held by a ישראל, דמאי, מעשר ראשון taken early on the stalks, and מעשר שני redeemed without the חומש. Finally it notes that only dry lupine may be moved, because moist lupine is too bitter even for animals.

steps.title: The extra items are part of acts of kindness
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that the extra items on the longer list fall under גמילות חסדים, which is already on the shorter list.
steps.simpleTranslation: These too (hospitality to guests and visiting the sick) belong to the category of acts of kindness.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers an earlier question: why does one list of rewarding מצוות have more items than the other? It says the extra items are really already included.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה's short list includes גמילות חסדים, acts of kindness. The ברייתא's longer list adds things like הכנסת אורחים and ביקור חולים. These are simply specific types of kindness, so the two lists do not really disagree.

phrases.english: These too,
phrases.notes: Refers to the extra items on the longer list, such as hospitality and visiting the sick.

phrases.english: belong to the category of acts of kindness.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question from the previous daf about why the two lists differ in length.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Inclusion: the extra items are sub-categories of an item already listed.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The longer list seems to add new מצוות that the משנה left out.
steps.terutzMaskana: The added items are forms of גמילות חסדים, so the משנה already covers them.

steps.title: A second version: the long-list items connect to the short-list items
steps.stepSummary: A different version of the answer says that each item on the longer list can be traced back to an item on the shorter list.
steps.simpleTranslation: A different version: these (the items on the longer list) are attributable to those (the items on the shorter list).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second version of the same answer, in more general wording.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first version said only that hospitality and visiting the sick fit under kindness. This version says something broader: every extra item on the long list belongs to some item on the short list. For example, early arrival at the בית המדרש connects to תלמוד תורה.

keyTerms.meaning: a different version (of the same answer)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not read this as a new argument against the first answer. 'לישנא אחרינא' is the same answer as it was handed down in a different form.

phrases.english: A different version:
these are attributable to those.
phrases.notes: 'These' means the long-list items; 'those' means the short-list items.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel version of the answer in Step 1, broader in scope.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Attribution: every long-list item maps onto a short-list item.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The lists might list different מצוות.
steps.terutzMaskana: All items on the long list are contained within the categories of the short list.
steps.whatToRemember: The two lists do not conflict. The longer list just spells out details that the shorter list already contains.

steps.title: One who judges others favorably is judged favorably
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that a person who gives others the benefit of the doubt will receive the same treatment from Heaven.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: One who judges his fellow favorably is himself judged favorably.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא about דן לכף זכות, one of the items on the longer list. This statement opens a new section.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The reward matches the deed (מידה כנגד מידה). If you look for the good explanation in other people's actions, Heaven will look for the good explanation in yours.

keyTerms.meaning: toward the side of merit, i.e. favorably

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the main teaching that the coming stories are meant to illustrate.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
One who judges his fellow favorably,
is himself judged favorably.
phrases.notes: He is judged this way by Heaven.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן הַדָּן חֲבֵירוֹ לְכַף זְכוּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Expands on one item from the longer list just discussed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Judging others favorably earns favorable judgment from Heaven.

steps.title: The worker asks for wages and is told 'I have nothing'
steps.stepSummary: A worker who served three years asks for his pay before יום הכיפורים. The employer says he has no money, produce, land, animals, or bedding, and the worker goes home heartbroken.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a story about a man from the Upper Galilee who was hired by a homeowner in the South for three years. On the eve of יום הכיפורים he said: 'Give me my wages so I can go and feed my wife and children.' The homeowner said: 'I have no money.' The worker said: 'Give me produce.' He said: 'I have none.' 'Give me land.' 'I have none.' 'Give me animals.' 'I have none.' 'Give me cushions and blankets.' 'I have none.' The worker slung his tools behind him and went home in anguish.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא begins a story that shows the teaching in action. This part sets up the test: the worker hears 'no' to everything.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worker keeps offering easier ways to be paid, and each one is refused. Any normal person would suspect the employer of cheating him. That is exactly what makes his later favorable judgment so impressive.

phrases.english: And there was an incident with a certain man
who came down from the Upper Galilee
and was hired by a certain homeowner
in the South for three years.
On the eve of Yom Kippur he said to him:
Give me my wages,
and I will go and feed my wife and children.
He said to him: I have no money.
He said to him: Give me produce.
He said to him: I have none.
Give me land. I have none.
Give me animals. I have none.

phrases.aramaic: תֵּן לִי כָּרִים וּכְסָתוֹת — אֵין לִי.
phrases.english: Give me cushions and blankets. I have none.
He slung his tools behind him,
and went home in anguish.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the illustrative story for the ברייתא's teaching.
steps.raayaObject: The teaching that one who judges favorably is judged favorably.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A מעשה (true story) brought within the ברייתא.

steps.title: The employer arrives with wages and gifts
steps.stepSummary: After סוכות, the employer brings the wages himself, along with three donkey-loads of food, drink, and sweets. After a meal, he pays.
steps.simpleTranslation: After the festival, the homeowner took the wages in his hand, along with three donkey-loads: one of food, one of drink, and one of sweets. He went to the worker's home. After they ate and drank, he gave him his wages.
steps.whatsHappening: The story continues: the employer comes in person and pays generously. This sets up the questions in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now it becomes clear that the employer was never trying to cheat the worker. He also adds extra gifts. This shows that the worker's earlier trust was justified.

phrases.english: After the festival
the homeowner took his wages in his hand,
and with him a load for three donkeys,

phrases.aramaic: אֶחָד שֶׁל מַאֲכָל, וְאֶחָד שֶׁל מִשְׁתֶּה,
phrases.english: one of food, and one of drink,
and one of kinds of sweets,
and went to his (the worker's) home.
After they ate and drank,
he gave him his wages.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְאַחַר הָרֶגֶל נָטַל בַּעַל הַבַּיִת שְׂכָרוֹ בְּיָדוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story: the employer follows through.

steps.title: What did you suspect about the money and the animals?
steps.stepSummary: The employer asks what the worker thought when he refused money and animals. The worker gave innocent explanations both times.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: 'When you said "Give me my wages" and I said "I have no money," what did you suspect me of?' The worker said: 'I thought perhaps a bargain on merchandise came your way and you bought it with the money.' 'And when you said "Give me animals" and I said "I have no animals," what did you suspect me of?' 'I thought perhaps they were rented out to others.'
steps.whatsHappening: The employer tests the worker, asking what he thought each time he heard 'no'. The worker's answers show he always found a favorable explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worker could easily have thought 'he is lying to avoid paying me.' Instead, he imagined real-life reasons. A sudden business deal would have used up the cash, and rented-out animals cannot be handed over.

keyTerms.meaning: what did you suspect me of?

steps.confusionAlert: The worker is not claiming he knew these reasons were true. He is choosing to assume a good explanation. That choice is what דן לכף זכות means.

phrases.english: He said to him: When you said to me
'Give me my wages'
and I said 'I have no money',
what did you suspect me of?
I said: Perhaps merchandise at a bargain price
came your way, and you bought it with the money.
And when you said to me 'Give me animals',
and I said 'I have no animals',
what did you suspect me of?
I said: Perhaps they are rented out to others.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back over each refusal from Step 4 to reveal the worker's favorable thoughts.
steps.raayaObject: That the worker truly judged his employer favorably.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The worker's own explanations within the מעשה.

steps.title: What did you suspect about the land, produce, and bedding?
steps.stepSummary: The worker explains that he thought the land was leased out, the produce was untithed, and the employer had dedicated all his property to the Temple.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'When you said "Give me land" and I said "I have no land," what did you suspect me of?' 'I thought perhaps it was leased to others.' 'And when I said "I have no produce," what did you suspect me of?' 'I thought perhaps it was not tithed.' 'And when I said "I have no cushions and blankets," what did you suspect me of?' 'I thought perhaps he had consecrated all his property to Heaven.'
steps.whatsHappening: The questioning continues through the rest of the refusals. Each time, the worker had assumed an innocent reason. The story continues next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These are reasons that would make it impossible or forbidden to pay. Leased land cannot be taken from the tenant. Untithed produce (טבל) may not be given away for eating. Property that is הקדש belongs to the Temple. The last answer covers everything at once: if all the property was consecrated, nothing at all could be given.

keyTerms.meaning: leased out (for a share of crops)

steps.whyThisMatters: The final explanation, that the employer consecrated everything, sets up the next part of the story, where the employer reveals what actually happened.

phrases.english: When you said to me 'Give me land',
and I said to you 'I have no land',
what did you suspect me of?

phrases.aramaic: אָמַרְתִּי: שֶׁמָּא מוּחְכֶּרֶת בְּיַד אֲחֵרִים הִיא.
phrases.english: I said: Perhaps it is leased to others.
And when I said to you 'I have no produce',
what did you suspect me of?
I said: Perhaps they are not tithed.

phrases.aramaic: וּבְשָׁעָה שֶׁאָמַרְתִּי לְךָ ״אֵין לִי כָּרִים וּכְסָתוֹת״
phrases.english: And when I said to you 'I have no cushions and blankets',
what did you suspect me of?

phrases.aramaic: אָמַרְתִּי: שֶׁמָּא הִקְדִּישׁ כָּל נְכָסָיו לַשָּׁמַיִם.
phrases.english: I said: Perhaps he consecrated all his property to Heaven.
phrases.notes: The worker switches to 'he', describing what he thought to himself at the time.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁאָמַרְתָּ לִי תֵּן לִי קַרְקַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same question-and-answer pattern for the remaining refusals.
steps.raayaObject: That the worker judged favorably at every step.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The worker's explanations within the מעשה.
steps.whatToRemember: For every 'no', the worker found an innocent reason. This is the model of הדן חבירו לכף זכות, and the story's ending (next) will show how he was rewarded.

steps.title: The employer confirms the worker's guess was true
steps.stepSummary: The employer swears that he really had vowed all his property to the מקדש because his son did not learn תורה. Later the חכמים in the South released his vows.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: I swear by the Temple service, that is exactly what happened! I vowed away all my property because of my son הורקנוס, who was not learning תורה. When I came to my colleagues in the South, they released all my vows.
steps.whatsHappening: The employer reveals that the worker's last innocent guess was exactly right. He really had no property available to pay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worker guessed that everything had been dedicated to the מקדש, and that was the real reason. The employer had vowed his property so his son, who was not learning תורה, would not inherit it. Once the חכמים released the vow (התרת נדרים), the money became his again, and he came right away to pay.

keyTerms.meaning: "By the Temple service!", an oath meaning "I swear it's true"
I vowed away (made my property forbidden/dedicated)

steps.confusionAlert: The employer was not lying when he said "I have nothing." At that moment his property truly was not his to use, because of the vow. That is why the worker's favorable judgment turned out to be correct.

phrases.english: He said to him: By the Temple service! So it was.
I vowed away all my property
because of Hyrcanus, my son,
who did not engage in Torah study.
And when I came to my colleagues in the South,
they released all my vows for me.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Confirms the worker's final guess from Step 7 (all property dedicated to the מקדש) and explains how it was later undone.
steps.raayaObject: The ברייתא's teaching about judging favorably
steps.raayaSupportSource: The employer's sworn confirmation that the worker's innocent guess was the truth

steps.title: The employer's blessing: as you judged me, so may ה׳ judge you
steps.stepSummary: The employer blesses the worker that ה׳ should judge him favorably, just as he judged the employer favorably.
steps.simpleTranslation: And you: just as you judged me favorably, so may ה׳ judge you favorably.
steps.whatsHappening: The first story ends with the blessing that directly matches the ברייתא's lesson.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This line ties the story back to the rule from Step 3: whoever gives others the benefit of the doubt is treated the same way by Heaven. The reward matches the act exactly (מידה כנגד מידה).
steps.whatToRemember: The worker had five reasons to suspect his employer and judged him favorably every time. ה׳ rewards that with the same favorable judgment.

phrases.english: And you, just as you judged me favorably,
may ה׳ judge you favorably.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the first story by stating its lesson outright.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Judging others favorably earns favorable judgment from ה׳.

steps.title: A second story: the חסיד who redeemed a captive girl
steps.stepSummary: A new ברייתא tells of a חסיד who ransomed a Jewish girl. At the inn he had her sleep at his feet. The next morning he went to the מקוה and then taught his students.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: A pious man once ransomed a young Jewish girl from captivity. At the inn, he had her lie down at his feet. The next day he went down, immersed in a מקוה, and taught his students.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second story on the same theme. This step only sets up the two actions that could look suspicious; the explanation comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two things here could look bad. First, he kept a young woman sleeping right by him. Second, he went to the מקוה in the morning, which could suggest he had been with her. The story is built so the students had real grounds for suspicion.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
There was an incident with a certain pious man
who redeemed a young Jewish girl,
and at the inn he had her lie down at his feet.
The next day he went down and immersed
and taught his students.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new, parallel story that illustrates the same teaching from Step 3.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A second ברייתא story about a חסיד and his students

steps.title: First question: why did he keep the girl at his feet?
steps.stepSummary: The חסיד asks his students what they suspected when he had her sleep at his feet. They answer that he wanted to protect her from a student who might not be trustworthy.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: When I had her lie at my feet, what did you suspect me of? They said: We thought maybe there is a student among us whom the רבי does not fully trust, so he kept her close to protect her.
steps.whatsHappening: The חסיד tests his students about the first suspicious act, and they give an innocent explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of assuming the worst about their רבי, the students found a reason that actually makes him look good: he was guarding her. They even suspected one of themselves before suspecting him.

phrases.english: And he said to them:
When I had her lie at my feet,
of what did you suspect me?
We said: Perhaps there is a student among us
who is not proven trustworthy to the Rebbe.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁהִשְׁכַּבְתִּיהָ תַּחַת מַרְגְּלוֹתַי, בַּמֶּה חֲשַׁדְתּוּנִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Addresses the first suspicious act from Step 10.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The students' innocent reading of the first act

steps.title: Second question: why did he go to the מקוה?
steps.stepSummary: The חסיד asks what they suspected when he went to the מקוה. They answer that perhaps the hard journey caused a קרי, which required immersion.
steps.simpleTranslation: When I went down and immersed, what did you suspect me of? They said: We thought maybe because of the strain of the journey, the רבי had a seminal emission (קרי).
steps.whatsHappening: The חסיד tests them about the second, even more suspicious act, and again they give an innocent reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Going to the מקוה in the morning could suggest he had been with the girl. The students explained it with a natural cause instead: travel exhaustion can bring on a קרי, and after a קרי one immerses before learning תורה.

keyTerms.meaning: a seminal emission, after which one immerses before learning

phrases.english: When I went down and immersed,
of what did you suspect me?
We said: Perhaps because of the strain of the journey
an emission befell the Rebbe.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Same pattern as Step 11, applied to the second suspicious act.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The students' innocent reading of the second act

steps.title: The חסיד confirms and blesses his students
steps.stepSummary: The חסיד swears that their guess was correct and blesses them that ה׳ should judge them favorably, just as they judged him.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: By the Temple service, that is exactly what happened! And you: just as you judged me favorably, may ה׳ judge you favorably.
steps.whatsHappening: The second story ends exactly like the first: an oath that the favorable guess was true, followed by the matching blessing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both stories share the same shape: actions that look suspicious, innocent explanations, a confirmation, and the blessing. Together they show the ברייתא's rule in action. Note the phrasing here is לכף זכות, "to the side of merit," the classic wording of this teaching.

keyTerms.meaning: to the scale of merit, i.e., giving the benefit of the doubt

steps.whatToRemember: Two stories, one lesson: when someone's action can be read innocently, read it that way, and ה׳ will judge you the same way.

phrases.english: He said to them: By the Temple service! So it was.
And you, just as you judged me favorably,
may ה׳ judge you favorably.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Confirms the students' answers from Steps 11–12 and closes the second story.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Judging others favorably earns favorable judgment from ה׳, as shown by both stories.

steps.title: A new story: the חכמים need help from a Roman matron
steps.stepSummary: A new ברייתא opens. The חכמים need something from a matron who is close to all the leaders of Rome, and רבי יהושע volunteers to go.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: Once the תלמידי חכמים needed something from a certain matron, whom all the great men of Rome used to visit. They said: Who will go? רבי יהושע said to them: I will go.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a third story, a ברייתא, about judging others favorably. This step only sets the scene for the story that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No suspicious act has happened yet. We learn why רבי יהושע went to her: she had influence with the Roman leaders, so the חכמים needed her help. This background matters later, because it gives an innocent reason for a private meeting.

keyTerms.meaning: The Rabbis taught. This phrase opens a ברייתא, a teaching from the time of the משנה that is not in the משנה itself.
A matron, meaning a noblewoman of high standing
The great men of Rome, meaning the powerful leaders of the government

steps.confusionAlert: This is a new story, not a continuation of the story about the חסיד and the girl. The topic is the same, which is judging people favorably, but the characters and events are new.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
Once, a certain matter was needed
by the Torah scholars, from a certain matron
whom all the great men of Rome would frequently visit.
They said: Who will go?

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לָהֶם רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ: אֲנִי אֵלֵךְ.
phrases.english: Rabbi Yehoshua said to them: I will go.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: פַּעַם אַחַת הוּצְרַךְ דָּבָר אֶחָד לְתַלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a third ברייתא story, after the worker and the חסיד, that illustrates the same teaching from Step 3: judging others favorably.
steps.raayaObject: The value of judging others favorably (דן לכף זכות)
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about רבי יהושע and the Roman matron

steps.title: רבי יהושע's actions that could look suspicious
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע removes his תפילין before entering, locks the door behind him, and afterward immerses before teaching his students.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהושע and his students went. When he reached the entrance of her house, he took off his תפילין four אמות away. Then he went in and locked the door in front of them. After he came out, he went down, immersed, and taught his students.
steps.whatsHappening: The story lists three actions by רבי יהושע that an onlooker might misread. This step sets up the questions he will ask his students next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each action could look bad on its own. Taking off תפילין, being alone behind a locked door with a woman, and then immersing could suggest something improper happened. The ברייתא lists them in order so that each one can be explained.

keyTerms.meaning: Four cubits, roughly six to eight feet

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehoshua and his students went.
As soon as he reached the entrance of her house,
he removed his tefillin at a distance of four cubits,
and he entered and locked the door in front of them.
After he came out,
he went down, immersed, and taught his students.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story by describing the actions that could raise suspicion.
steps.raayaObject: The value of judging others favorably (דן לכף זכות)
steps.raayaSupportSource: The actions of רבי יהושע in the ברייתא

steps.title: The students explain why he removed his tefillin
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע asks what they thought when he took off his תפילין. They answer that he did not want holy objects to enter an impure place.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: When I took off my תפילין, what did you suspect me of? They answered: We said that our teacher holds that holy things should not enter a place of impurity.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע tests his students about the first suspicious action. They give an innocent and respectful explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Removing תפילין could have looked like preparing for something improper. The students instead assumed a holy reason: the matron's house, the home of a non-Jewish woman, was a place of impurity, so it was not fitting to bring תפילין inside.

keyTerms.meaning: What did you suspect me of?
Holy things, here meaning the תפילין
A place of impurity, meaning the home of a non-Jewish noblewoman

phrases.english: And he said to them:
When I removed my tefillin, what did you suspect me of?
We said: The Rabbi must hold

phrases.aramaic: לֹא יִכָּנְסוּ דִּבְרֵי קְדוּשָּׁה בִּמְקוֹם טוּמְאָה.
phrases.english: that holy things should not enter a place of impurity.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the first suspicious action from step 15.
steps.raayaObject: The students judged their teacher favorably
steps.raayaSupportSource: The students' explanation about the תפילין

steps.title: The students explain why he locked the door
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע asks what they thought when he locked the door. They answer that perhaps there was a secret government matter between him and the matron.
steps.simpleTranslation: When I locked the door, what did you suspect me of? They answered: We said that perhaps there was a matter of the government between him and her.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע tests his students about the second suspicious action, being alone with a woman behind a locked door. They again give an innocent explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Being locked in a room with a woman could look like a serious sin. The students instead assumed a political reason: confidential government business had to stay private. This fits the background from step 14, since she had influence with the Roman leaders. The question about the immersion comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: A matter of the government, meaning confidential political business
Between him and her, meaning in private

phrases.english: When I locked the door, what did you suspect me of?
We said: Perhaps a matter of the government
is between him and her.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the second suspicious action from step 15, locking the door.
steps.raayaObject: The students judged their teacher favorably
steps.raayaSupportSource: The students' explanation about the locked door

steps.title: The students explain why he immersed
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע asks his third question, about his immersion. The students answer that perhaps the matron's spittle sprayed onto his clothes.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהושע asked: 'When I went down and immersed, what did you suspect me of?' They said: 'We said that perhaps a bit of spittle sprayed from her mouth onto the clothes of our רבי.'
steps.whatsHappening: This is the third and final question in the story. The students again give a kind, innocent explanation for what they saw.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Immersing after a visit to a woman could look suspicious. The students explain it with a הלכה instead: חכמים decreed that a non-Jew's bodily fluids, like spittle, make things impure like a זב. So he needed to immerse because of טומאה, not because of any sin.

keyTerms.meaning: a spray or drop of spittle

steps.confusionAlert: The spittle makes him impure only because of a rabbinic decree that treats non-Jews like a זב. It has nothing to do with any improper behavior.

phrases.english: At the time that I went down and immersed
of what did you suspect me?
We said: perhaps a spray of spittle shot out
from her mouth onto the clothes of the Rabbi.
phrases.notes: A non-Jew's spittle is impure by rabbinic decree, like that of a זב.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The third question-and-answer, following the questions about the תפילין and the locked door.
steps.raayaObject: That one must judge others favorably (דן לכף זכות)
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא about רבי יהושע and his students

steps.title: רבי יהושע swears they were right and blesses them
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע swears by the Temple service that their guess was correct and blesses them that ה׳ should judge them favorably.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: 'By the Temple service, that is how it was! And you, just as you judged me favorably, may ה׳ judge you favorably.'
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends. רבי יהושע confirms that their kind guesses were true and gives them a blessing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This closing matches the endings of the worker story (Step 9) and the חסיד story (Step 13). All three stories show the reward of judging others favorably: the one who judges kindly is judged kindly by ה׳, measure for measure.

keyTerms.meaning: 'By the Temple service!' (a form of oath)

steps.whatToRemember: All three stories teach the same lesson: whoever judges others favorably will be judged favorably by ה׳.

phrases.english: He said to them: By the Temple service!
That is how it was.
And you, just as you judged me favorably,
may the Omnipresent judge you favorably.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Confirms the students' answers and closes the story.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Judging others favorably brings ה׳'s favorable judgment.

steps.title: Moving pure terumah seems obvious
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the משנה, which allows moving pure תרומה on שבת, and asks why this needed to be said.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'One may move pure תרומה, etc.' But that is obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the list in the משנה and questions the first item. It is setting up an answer that will explain why the משנה needed to say it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Pure תרומה is real food that a כהן may eat, so it is clearly not מוקצה. The question is: why would the משנה bother to teach something so plain?

keyTerms.meaning: we may clear away or move (on שבת)
ritually pure תרומה, which a כהן may eat

phrases.english: One may move pure terumah, etc.
That is obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the stories and returns to the משנה's list of items that may be moved.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that pure תרומה may be moved
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Food that is fit to eat is obviously not מוקצה, so the ruling seems unnecessary.

steps.title: Terumah held by a non-kohen may still be moved
steps.stepSummary: The משנה is needed for the case where the תרומה is with a ישראל, who may not eat it. Since a כהן may eat it, the ישראל may still move it.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is needed only where the תרומה is in a ישראל's possession. You might have said that since he cannot eat it, he may not move it. So the משנה teaches us that since it is fit for a כהן, it is fine to move it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the משנה is speaking about a ישראל who has תרומה in his house.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before this answer, we might have thought something is מוקצה if the person holding it cannot eat it. The answer teaches that it is enough for the item to be fit for someone. Because a כהן can eat it, it is not מוקצה even for the ישראל.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed only for (a specific case)

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a key rule of מוקצה: an item that is usable by some people is not מוקצה, even for someone who cannot use it himself.

phrases.english: It is necessary only where it is placed in the hands of an Israelite.
You might have said:
since it is not fit for him, it is forbidden;
it teaches us
that since it is fit for a priest, it is fine.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'obvious' question by narrowing the case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since the ישראל cannot eat it, it would be מוקצה for him.
steps.terutzMaskana: Since it is fit for a כהן, anyone may move it.

steps.title: How can demai be moved if he cannot eat it?
steps.stepSummary: The משנה allows moving דמאי, but the owner is not allowed to eat it before tithing, so why isn't it מוקצה?
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'And דמאי, etc.' But דמאי is not fit for him!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the next item in the משנה, דמאי. It is setting up an explanation of why דמאי is not מוקצה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Separating מעשרות is forbidden on שבת, so the owner cannot fix the דמאי and eat it today. If it is unusable for him, it should be מוקצה.

keyTerms.meaning: produce bought from an עם הארץ, which may not have been tithed
but it is not fit for him!

phrases.english: And demai, etc.
Demai? But it is not fit for him!

steps.triggerLanguage: וּדְמַאי וְכוּ׳. דְּמַאי, הָא לָא חֲזֵי לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next item in the משנה's list.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that דמאי may be moved
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Food the owner cannot eat should be מוקצה.

steps.title: He could make himself poor, so demai counts as fit
steps.stepSummary: If he wanted, he could declare all his property ownerless and become poor. A poor person may eat דמאי, so it counts as fit for him even now.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since, if he wanted, he could make all his property ownerless and become a poor person, and then the דמאי would be fit for him, it is fit for him now too.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that דמאי counts as usable because the owner always has a way to become allowed to eat it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer depends on the idea that a poor person may eat דמאי. Since the owner could make himself poor at any moment by giving up his property, the דמאי is potentially fit for him. Because of that, it is not מוקצה.
steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא does not mean that he actually gives away his property. The mere fact that he could do so is enough to make the דמאי count as fit for him.

phrases.english: Since if he wants,
he can declare his property ownerless
and become a poor man, and it would be fit for him,
now too it is fit for him.

steps.triggerLanguage: כֵּיוָן דְּאִי בָּעֵי מַפְקַר לֵיהּ לְנִכְסֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge about דמאי.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Potential fitness: he could become poor
steps.terutzHavaAmina: דמאי is unfit for the owner and therefore מוקצה.
steps.terutzMaskana: Because he could become poor and eat it, it counts as fit now.

steps.title: Proof: the poor may be fed demai
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a משנה stating that the poor and soldiers may be fed דמאי.
steps.simpleTranslation: As we learned in a משנה: One may feed the poor דמאי, and soldiers דמאי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proves the idea from the last step, that a poor person is allowed to eat דמאי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Tithing דמאי is only a rabbinic stringency, and חכמים did not apply it to the poor. This משנה supports the answer in Step 23.

keyTerms.meaning: as we learned in a משנה

phrases.english: As we learned: One may feed the poor demai
and soldiers demai.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Provides a source for the claim that a poor person may eat דמאי.
steps.raayaObject: That a poor person may eat דמאי

steps.title: רב הונא: this ruling follows בית הלל
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא cites a ברייתא showing that בית שמאי forbid feeding the poor דמאי, while בית הלל permit it. The משנה follows בית הלל.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב הונא said: It was taught: בית שמאי say that one may not feed the poor or soldiers דמאי. And בית הלל say that one may feed the poor and soldiers דמאי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds that the ruling permitting the poor to eat דמאי was actually a disagreement, and it is the view of בית הלל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This shows that the ruling in Step 24 is not undisputed. Since the הלכה follows בית הלל, the idea that the poor may eat דמאי still stands, and so does the answer about moving דמאי on שבת.
steps.whatToRemember: דמאי is not מוקצה because the owner could become poor, and the poor may eat דמאי according to בית הלל.

phrases.english: And Rav Huna said: It was taught:

phrases.aramaic: בֵּית שַׁמַּאי אוֹמְרִים: אֵין מַאֲכִילִין אֶת הָעֲנִיִּים דְּמַאי
phrases.english: Beit Shammai say: One may not feed the poor demai
nor soldiers demai.

phrases.aramaic: וּבֵית הִלֵּל אוֹמְרִים: מַאֲכִילִין אֶת הָעֲנִיִּים דְּמַאי
phrases.english: And Beit Hillel say: One may feed the poor demai
and soldiers demai.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַב הוּנָא: תָּנָא, בֵּית שַׁמַּאי אוֹמְרִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Identifies the source of the משנה's view as בית הלל.
steps.raayaObject: That the ruling allowing the poor to eat דמאי follows בית הלל
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא cited by רב הונא

steps.title: Moving first tithe seems obvious
steps.stepSummary: The משנה allows moving מעשר ראשון whose תרומה was already taken. The גמרא asks why this is not obvious.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'And מעשר ראשון whose תרומה was taken, etc.' But that is obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the next item in the משנה. It is setting up the case that explains why the משנה needed to mention it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once תרומת מעשר is taken, the מעשר ראשון is fully permitted food (חולין). So why would anyone think it is מוקצה?

keyTerms.meaning: first tithe, given to a לוי
its תרומה, meaning the תרומת מעשר

phrases.english: And first tithe whose terumah was taken, etc.
That is obvious!

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמַעֲשֵׂר רִאשׁוֹן שֶׁנִּיטְּלָה תְּרוּמָתוֹ וְכוּ׳. פְּשִׁיטָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next item in the משנה's list.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling about מעשר ראשון
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Tithed produce is plain permitted food, so of course it may be moved.

steps.title: The case where the Levite took the tithe while still on the stalks
steps.stepSummary: The משנה means a case where the לוי took his מעשר early, while the grain was still on the stalks. Only תרומת מעשר was taken from it, not תרומה גדולה.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is needed only where the לוי took it early, while the grain was still on the stalks. תרומת מעשר was taken from it, but תרומה גדולה was not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the special case the משנה is talking about. The next step brings the source for why this case is exempt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally תרומה גדולה is taken first. Here it was never taken, so you might think the מעשר is still טבל and therefore מוקצה. The משנה teaches that it may be moved, because מעשר taken this early is exempt from תרומה גדולה.

keyTerms.meaning: he (the לוי) took it ahead of the כהן
the tenth of the מעשר that the לוי gives to a כהן
the main תרומה, normally taken first from the crop

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think this מעשר is טבל because תרומה גדולה was never taken. When the לוי takes his share before the grain is threshed, it is exempt from תרומה גדולה.

phrases.english: It is necessary only where he took it early, while still on the stalks,
and the terumah of the tithe was taken from it,
but the great terumah was not taken from it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'obvious' question by describing an unusual case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since תרומה גדולה was never taken, the מעשר is טבל and מוקצה.
steps.terutzMaskana: מעשר taken while the grain is still on the stalks is exempt from תרומה גדולה, so it may be moved.

steps.title: ריש לקיש: tithe taken on the stalks is exempt from the big teruma
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא supports its explanation with a teaching of רבי אבהו in the name of ריש לקיש. מעשר ראשון that the לוי took early, while the grain was still on the stalks, is exempt from תרומה גדולה. The verse says only 'a tithe from the tithe,' meaning only תרומת מעשר is required.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this fits what רבי אבהו said in the name of ריש לקיש: if the לוי took his מעשר ראשון early, while the grain was still on the stalks, it is exempt from תרומה גדולה. The verse says, 'You shall set apart from it a gift for ה׳, a tithe from the tithe.' God is saying: I told you to take a tithe from the tithe, not both תרומה גדולה and תרומת מעשר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a source to show that the case from step 27 is real. Tithe that was taken early truly owes only תרומת מעשר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The usual order is that the כהן's תרומה גדולה is taken first, then the לוי's מעשר ראשון, and then the לוי gives תרומת מעשר. Here the לוי got there first, before the grain was even threshed. The verse 'a tithe from the tithe' tells us that in this case the לוי gives only תרומת מעשר, so the leftover tithe is fully usable and may be moved on שבת.

keyTerms.meaning: First tithe, the tenth of the crop given to the לוי
He took it early, before the כהן's share was separated
Stalks or ears of grain, before threshing
The 'big' תרומה, the first gift given to the כהן
The tenth of his tithe that the לוי gives to the כהן

steps.whyThisMatters: This explains why the משנה needed to say this case: the tithe is fully permitted even though תרומה גדולה was never taken from it.

phrases.english: And it is like that which Rabbi Abbahu said
Reish Lakish said:
First tithe that he (the Levite) took early, while still on the stalks
is exempt from the big teruma,
as it says: 'And you shall set apart from it'
'a gift for ה׳, a tithe from the tithe.'
A tithe from the tithe I told you to take,
and not the big teruma
plus the teruma of the tithe from the tithe.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the case definition given in step 27 with a teaching of an אמורא.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that tithe taken early on the stalks needs only תרומת מעשר
steps.raayaSupportSource: ריש לקיש's reading of the verse 'מעשר מן המעשר' (במדבר יח:כו)

steps.title: רב פפא: then tithe taken early from the pile should also be exempt
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא asks אביי: if the לוי who gets there first is exempt, he should also be exempt when he took his tithe from the threshed pile.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said to אביי: If so, even if the לוי took it early from the pile, he should also be exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא challenges ריש לקיש's rule. If the verse frees the early לוי from תרומה גדולה, why should it matter whether the grain was on the stalks or already in a pile?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse 'a tithe from the tithe' does not mention stalks at all. So the reasoning seems to apply to any case where the לוי took his tithe before the כהן, including after threshing. רב פפא wants to know what limits the rule to stalks.

keyTerms.meaning: A pile of threshed and winnowed grain
If so (a challenge built on what was just said)

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said to Abaye:
If so, even if he took it early from the pile
he should also be exempt!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, אֲפִילּוּ הִקְדִּימוֹ בִּכְרִי נָמֵי לִיפְּטַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reach of ריש לקיש's rule from step 28.
steps.kashyaTarget: ריש לקיש's exemption of early tithe from תרומה גדולה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The verse's reasoning should apply equally to tithe taken early from the pile, yet that case is obligated.

steps.title: אביי: a different verse obligates the pile case
steps.stepSummary: אביי answers that the verse 'From all your gifts you shall set apart' requires תרומה גדולה from the tithe in the pile case.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: About your case, the verse says, 'From all your gifts you shall set apart ה׳'s תרומה.'
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers that a second verse obligates the לוי to give תרומה גדולה when he took his tithe from the pile.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse 'מכל מתנותיכם' teaches that ה׳'s תרומה, meaning תרומה גדולה, must be taken from all the לוי's gifts. So there are two verses. One exempts the לוי and one obligates him, and each must apply to a different case.

keyTerms.meaning: About your case the verse says

phrases.english: He said to him: About you (your case) the verse says:
'From all your gifts you shall set apart,' etc.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב פפא's challenge from step 29.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Brings a separate verse that covers the pile case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The early לוי is always exempt, even when he took from the pile
steps.terutzMaskana: The verse 'מכל מתנותיכם' obligates the pile case in תרומה גדולה

steps.title: Why apply each verse to that particular case?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what made us apply the obligating verse to the pile and the exempting verse to the stalks, and not the other way around.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what did you see? Why did you decide this way?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges how the two verses were divided between the cases. This sets up the next step, which gives the reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now there are two verses, one exempting and one obligating. Nothing yet tells us why the stalks get the exemption and the pile gets the obligation. The גמרא wants a reason for the split.

keyTerms.meaning: And what did you see? (Why did you choose this way?)

phrases.english: And what did you see (to decide this way)?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the way step 30 divided the two verses.
steps.kashyaTarget: The division between the exempting verse (stalks) and the obligating verse (pile)
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Without a reason, the verses could just as well be applied the other way around.

steps.title: Piled grain is already 'grain'; grain on the stalks is not yet
steps.stepSummary: Grain in a pile has already become 'דגן,' so the כהן's share has taken hold. Grain still on the stalks has not yet become דגן.
steps.simpleTranslation: This one (the pile) has become grain, and that one (on the stalks) has not become grain.
steps.whatsHappening: The answer explains the split. Once grain is threshed and piled, it counts as 'grain,' and the כהן's right to תרומה גדולה has already taken effect.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah calls תרומה 'ראשית דגנך,' the first of your grain. Once the grain is in a pile it is called דגן, so the obligation of תרומה גדולה is already in place and the לוי cannot take it away by grabbing his tithe first. On the stalks, it is not yet דגן, so the לוי's early tithe is taken before the obligation exists.

keyTerms.meaning: It has become grain (דגן), fully processed
Grain, the stage when the duty of תרומה takes hold

steps.whatToRemember: Tithe taken early on the stalks owes only תרומת מעשר. Tithe taken early from the pile also owes תרומה גדולה, because by then the grain is already 'דגן.'

phrases.english: This one (in the pile) has become grain,
and that one (on the stalks) has not become grain.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question from step 31.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Draws a line based on the stage of the produce
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The verses could be applied either way
steps.terutzMaskana: The obligation begins once the grain becomes דגן in the pile, so only the stalks case is exempt

steps.title: Moving redeemed second tithe seems obvious
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה, which allows moving redeemed מעשר שני, and asks why this needs to be said.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'And מעשר שני, etc.' That is obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to the next part of the משנה. It asks why the משנה needed to say this at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once מעשר שני has been redeemed, it is plain חולין and can be eaten anywhere. So of course it may be moved on שבת. The גמרא asks what new thing the משנה is teaching.

keyTerms.meaning: Second tithe, eaten in ירושלים or redeemed for money

phrases.english: 'And second tithe, etc.' (quoting the mishna)
It is obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next clause of the משנה, following the same 'why say it?' pattern as step 26.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's clause permitting the moving of redeemed מעשר שני
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Redeemed tithe is plain חולין, so allowing it to be moved teaches nothing new.

steps.title: Paid the principal but not the fifth: the fifth does not hold up redemption
steps.stepSummary: The משנה is speaking about someone who paid the main value but not the extra fifth. It teaches that the missing חומש does not hold back the redemption.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is needed only where he paid the main value but did not pay the fifth. This teaches us that the fifth does not hold back the redemption.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the new point in the משנה. Even if the owner still owes the added fifth, the tithe is already redeemed and may be moved.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An owner who redeems his own מעשר שני must add a fifth (חומש). You might think that until he pays the fifth, the tithe is still holy. The משנה teaches that paying the principal alone makes it חולין, and the fifth is a separate debt.

keyTerms.meaning: The principal, the main value of the item
The added fifth an owner pays when redeeming his own holy item
Holds back, prevents something from taking effect
It is needed only for (this case)

steps.whatToRemember: Redemption of מעשר שני takes effect once the principal is paid. The missing חומש does not hold it back.
steps.confusionAlert: The חומש is still owed. The point is only that not paying it yet does not stop the tithe from becoming חולין.

phrases.english: It is needed only where he gave the principal
but did not give the fifth.
This teaches us
that the fifth does not hold back (the redemption).

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא צְרִיכָא שֶׁנָּתַן אֶת הַקֶּרֶן וְלֹא נָתַן אֶת הַחוֹמֶשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'it is obvious' challenge of step 33.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrows the case and shows the new law it teaches
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Until the fifth is paid, the tithe stays holy and may not be moved
steps.terutzMaskana: Paying the principal alone makes the tithe חולין, because the fifth does not hold back the redemption

steps.title: Only dry lupine may be moved, not moist lupine
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's mention of dry תורמוס and notes that the word 'dry' is exact. Moist lupine is not included in the permission.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says 'and dry lupine.' This means only dry lupine. But moist lupine may not be moved.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next line of the משנה, about dry lupine. It makes a careful point: the משנה said 'dry' on purpose, so moist lupine is not allowed. This sets up the question in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Dry lupine is too hard for people to eat, but the משנה permits moving it because goats eat it. From the word 'dry,' the גמרא learns a limit: moist lupine is excluded and may not be moved. Steps 36–37 give the reason for this limit.

keyTerms.meaning: Specifically, exactly this and nothing else

steps.confusionAlert: Do not assume that moist food is always more edible. Here the moist lupine is the one that may not be moved, because it is too bitter even for animals.

phrases.english: And the dry lupine, etc.
phrases.notes: A quote from the next line of the משנה. Dry lupine may be moved because it is goat food.

phrases.english: Specifically dry,
phrases.notes: The word 'dry' in the משנה is exact.

phrases.english: but moist, no.
phrases.notes: Moist lupine may not be moved.

steps.alternativePossibleLabel: דיוק (inference from the wording of the משנה)
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from the מעשר שני line of the משנה (steps 33–34) to the next case in the משנה, dry lupine.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Only dry lupine may be moved on שבת as animal food. Moist lupine may not be moved.

steps.title: Why is moist lupine excluded?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reason that moist lupine may not be moved.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why moist lupine is forbidden to move. This question sets up the explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is not an attack. It is a request for the reasoning behind the limit found in step 35. We might have thought moist lupine should be allowed even more easily than dry lupine, so the גמרא wants to know what makes it different.

phrases.english: What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind the limit found in step 35.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason why moist lupine may not be moved, even though dry lupine may be.

steps.title: Moist lupine is too bitter for animals to eat
steps.stepSummary: Moist lupine is bitter, so an animal will not eat it. That means it does not count as animal food and may not be moved.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since it is bitter, an animal will not eat it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that moist lupine is too bitter for an animal to eat. So it is not useful as animal food and stays forbidden to move on שבת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Something may be moved on שבת only if it has a use, and here that use is animal food. Dry lupine is not bitter in this way, so goats eat it and it may be moved. Moist lupine is bitter, so even animals refuse it, and it has no use that would permit moving it.

keyTerms.meaning: Something set aside from use, which may not be moved on שבת

steps.whatToRemember: An item may be moved on שבת as food only if someone, whether a person or an animal, will actually eat it. Dry lupine passes this test because goats eat it. Moist lupine fails because it is too bitter even for animals.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows the general rule of food and מוקצה: being fit to eat depends on whether people or animals really eat the item in its present state.

phrases.english: Since it is bitter,
it (an animal) will not eat it.
phrases.notes: So it is not animal food and may not be moved.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 36.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Moist lupine is bitter, so animals will not eat it. It therefore has no food use and may not be moved.
